newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S.- held Hamas leader would welcome Jordan deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S.- held Hamas leader would welcome Jordan deal.

text.p: The leader of the Palestinian militant group Hamas, who is awaiting extradition from the United States to Israel, would welcome a deal to send him instead to Jordan, his lawyer said on Thursday.

Security sources confirmed an Israeli newspaper report on Wednesday that Israeli, Jordanian and U.S. officials were secretly examining a deal to send Mousa Abu Marzook to Amman in return for a promise to shun violence.
Israel had alleged that Abu Marzook, as political leader of the Islamic militant group, was responsible for attacks that killed scores of Israelis. It demanded his extradition.

Abu Marzook had said he was involved only in political matters for which he could not be extradited. But last month, after 18 months in a New York jail, he dropped his court challenge to Israel's demand that U.S. officials hand him over.

"He feels that he is a sort of a pawn in the politics of whatever is going on and...got to the point where he was resigned and said fine, if that's the game I go back to Israel, face whatever there is to it," his lawyer Cherif Bassiouni said.

"So I am sure if somebody said, you know, go to Jordan or go to Gaza or go to Egypt or stay in the U.S. I am sure these options would be welcomed by him," Bassiouni told Israel Radio from New York in an interview broadcast on Thursday.
A lawyer for Abu Marzook said last month he feared that Abu Marzook would be tortured or possibly killed in Israel.

Israeli justice officials declined comment on the deal reported by the daily Yedioth Ahronoth. But the newspaper said Israeli intelligence officials wanted to send him to Jordan for fear of a wave of Hamas attacks should he arrive in Israel.
"There are contacts and they're examining the possibility of sending him to Jordan," an Israeli security source said on Thursday.
Hamas has warned of guerrilla attacks should Abu Marzook be extradited to the Jewish state. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has asked the United States not to send him to Israel.
Bassiouni said he believed Abu Marzook would have no problem signing a statement promising to shun violence. The lawyer told the radio: "He has never advocated violence to the best of my knowledge.
"He has made several statements already saying, 'I urge my friends and followers not to engage in violence, asked them to remain calm,'" the lawyer said.

"As a political leader there is probably a limit to how far he can go and still retain a certain political credibility but I think that something like this could certainly be worked out," Bassiouni said.
